steps.title: Which orders supply the report?
steps.change: Each row in 🟦 `Orders` represents an order. `OrderID` identifies the order and `CustomerID` identifies its customer. Those two fields supply both grouping stages. The filter applies to the input orders before the first group forms.
steps.added_sql:
SELECT OrderID, CustomerID
FROM Orders
WHERE CustomerID IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY OrderID;
steps.sql:
SELECT OrderID, CustomerID
FROM Orders
WHERE CustomerID IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY OrderID;

steps.title: How many orders did each customer place?
steps.change: Group the four eligible orders by 🟦 `CustomerID`. Within each group, count its order IDs. The result has one row for each of the three identified customers.
steps.added_sql:
SELECT CustomerID, COUNT(OrderID) AS total_orders
-- …
GROUP BY CustomerID
ORDER BY CustomerID;
steps.sql:
SELECT CustomerID, COUNT(OrderID) AS total_orders
FROM Orders
WHERE CustomerID IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY CustomerID
ORDER BY CustomerID;

steps.title: Which label does the CTE give each customer?
steps.change: The `CASE` expression uses each group’s order count. A value of **1** gives `One-time`. Two or more gives `Repeat`. The final learner query calculates the count and the label in the same CTE.
steps.added_sql:
WITH customer_order_counts AS (
    SELECT
        CustomerID,
        COUNT(OrderID) AS total_orders,
        CASE
            WHEN COUNT(OrderID) = 1 THEN 'One-time'
            ELSE 'Repeat'
        END AS customer_type
-- …
)
SELECT CustomerID, total_orders, customer_type
FROM customer_order_counts
steps.sql:
WITH customer_order_counts AS (
    SELECT
        CustomerID,
        COUNT(OrderID) AS total_orders,
        CASE
            WHEN COUNT(OrderID) = 1 THEN 'One-time'
            ELSE 'Repeat'
        END AS customer_type
    FROM Orders
    WHERE CustomerID IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY CustomerID
)
SELECT CustomerID, total_orders, customer_type
FROM customer_order_counts
ORDER BY CustomerID;

steps.title: What does the main query count?
steps.change: Each row of the CTE is already one buyer. Buyers 10 and 30 are One-time, while buyer 20 is Repeat.
steps.added_sql: SELECT customer_type, COUNT(total_orders) AS customers FROM customer_order_counts GROUP BY customer_type;
steps.sql:
WITH customer_order_counts AS (
    SELECT
        CustomerID,
        COUNT(OrderID) AS total_orders,
        CASE
            WHEN COUNT(OrderID) = 1 THEN 'One-time'
            ELSE 'Repeat'
        END AS customer_type
    FROM Orders
    WHERE CustomerID IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY CustomerID
)

SELECT customer_type, COUNT(total_orders) AS customers FROM customer_order_counts GROUP BY customer_type;

steps.title: Count all ordering customers
steps.change: The scalar denominator reads all three customer rows. It gives both groups the same benchmark of three customers.
steps.added_sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS ordering_customers FROM customer_order_counts;
steps.sql:
WITH customer_order_counts AS (
    SELECT
        CustomerID,
        COUNT(OrderID) AS total_orders,
        CASE
            WHEN COUNT(OrderID) = 1 THEN 'One-time'
            ELSE 'Repeat'
        END AS customer_type
    FROM Orders
    WHERE CustomerID IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY CustomerID
)

SELECT COUNT(*) AS ordering_customers FROM customer_order_counts;

steps.title: Calculate each customer type’s percentage and sort
steps.change: The outer query counts customer rows within each type and divides by the three customers from the denominator branch. One-time gives 2 ÷ 3 × 100 = 66.67%, and Repeat gives 1 ÷ 3 × 100 = 33.33%. Sorting by customer_type puts One-time first.
steps.added_sql:
SELECT
    customer_type,
    COUNT(total_orders) AS customers,
    ROUND(
        COUNT(total_orders) * 100.0
        / (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customer_order_counts),
        2
    ) AS pct_of_customers
FROM customer_order_counts
GROUP BY customer_type
ORDER BY customer_type;
